clinicalPearls: An acute leukaemia of ambiguous lineage in which the blasts express antigens of more than one lineage, so they cannot be assigned to acute myeloid or acute lymphoblastic leukaemia alone.

Diagnosis follows strict immunophenotypic criteria: myeloid assignment requires myeloperoxidase or monocytic differentiation, T-lineage requires cytoplasmic CD3, and B-lineage requires strong CD19 with other B markers.
May present as a single blast population co-expressing markers (biphenotypic) or as two distinct blast populations (bilineal); both fall under the same category.
The commonest combinations are B-myeloid and T-myeloid; trilineage and T/B forms are rare.
Two recurrent genetic subtypes are recognised by definition: MPAL with BCR-ABL1 and MPAL with KMT2A (MLL) rearrangement, both of which must be actively excluded.
A firm diagnosis requires flow cytometry and cytochemistry across an adequate marker panel plus cytogenetic and molecular testing; misassignment changes treatment entirely.
Optimal therapy is not standardised, but ALL-based induction regimens are often favoured, with allogeneic stem-cell transplantation considered in first remission for many patients.
Presentation resembles other acute leukaemias, with marrow failure causing anaemia, bleeding, infection and often high blast counts.
reference.pathophysiology: Mixed phenotype acute leukaemia arises from transformation of an early haematopoietic progenitor, or from a leukaemic stem cell with lineage plasticity, before firm commitment to the myeloid, T-lymphoid or B-lymphoid programme. As a result the malignant clone co-expresses lineage-defining antigens of more than one pathway, either within a single blast population or as separate coexisting populations. Underlying this promiscuous phenotype are recurrent genetic lesions: BCR-ABL1 (the Philadelphia chromosome) produces a constitutively active tyrosine kinase, while KMT2A (MLL) rearrangements dysregulate developmental transcription programmes that maintain progenitors in a lineage-ambiguous state; other cases carry alterations in genes such as ZNF384, PHF6, WT1, RUNX1 and various epigenetic regulators. These events lock cells at a stage where the transcriptional networks that normally enforce a single lineage identity are disrupted, permitting simultaneous myeloid and lymphoid gene expression. Uncontrolled proliferation of these blasts replaces normal marrow, producing pancytopenia, and the tumour's mixed identity is what defies classification into a single conventional acute leukaemia category and complicates treatment selection.
additionalDifferentials: Acute myeloid leukaemia with aberrant lymphoid antigen expression
Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (B or T) with aberrant myeloid marker expression
Early T-cell precursor acute lymphoblastic leukaemia
Blast phase of chronic myeloid leukaemia (especially with BCR-ABL1)
Lineage switch at relapse of a previously assigned acute leukaemia
additionalInvestigations: Comprehensive multiparameter flow cytometry covering myeloid, B- and T-lineage markers
Cytochemistry including myeloperoxidase and non-specific esterase
Cytogenetics and FISH for BCR-ABL1 and KMT2A (MLL) rearrangements
Molecular studies including BCR-ABL1 transcript and broad myeloid/lymphoid gene panels
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy with immunohistochemistry
Cerebrospinal fluid examination for central nervous system involvement
HLA typing and early referral for allogeneic transplant assessment
redFlags: Very high circulating blast count with leukostasis symptoms (breathlessness, visual or neurological changes)
Tumour lysis syndrome with metabolic derangement at presentation
Severe cytopenias causing bleeding or serious infection
Central nervous system symptoms suggesting leukaemic infiltration
Detection of BCR-ABL1, which changes management and prognosis
reference.prognosis: Mixed phenotype acute leukaemia generally carries a less favourable prognosis than lineage-defined acute leukaemias, particularly in adults and in cases with adverse cytogenetics such as BCR-ABL1 or KMT2A rearrangement. Outcomes are better in children, and allogeneic stem-cell transplantation in first remission improves survival for many patients.
pitfalls: Forcing the leukaemia into a single AML or ALL category and missing the mixed phenotype, leading to suboptimal therapy.
Over-diagnosing MPAL from minor aberrant antigen expression without meeting the strict lineage-assignment criteria.
Failing to test for BCR-ABL1 and KMT2A rearrangements, which are defining and treatment-altering.
Overlooking a lineage switch at relapse, mistaking it for a new second leukaemia.
Delaying transplant referral and HLA typing, given that many patients benefit from transplantation in first remission.
references: International consensus classification of acute leukaemias
